title: Bands of the late 1910s and the change to march-time rhythm
summary: He says other bands played ragtime and that he changed the rhythm in Chicago after seeing the Castles' dancing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I got ideas, these men, certainly I wasn't the only one, jada, jada, jada, jada, jingle dee, and all comes from the same kind of stuff. These tunes came after.
Well what about the bands in the late 1910s and the early 20s?
Well they all played right after they heard you on music. Wait a minute, 1910?

Well now, the bands, they played regular popular tunes. I never heard any numbers that was improvised or worked on. If they played a chorus of different tunes, they may have had a little bit flourishes to it with their own. I don't say they didn't do that, but they were playing ragtime. I played ragtime. And the rhythm wasn't changing until I hit Chicago. Now this is going to be a strange thing and this is why they say the miracle couldn't happen. There was a dance team called, wait a minute, the castles. And at the castles was bringing out a new dance, like a straight dance, like a walk. Now ragtime music would fit it. But I noticed the general public. It was hard for them with the methods of music we were playing, that jumping music. So I decided to play in march time. Slow down, making a fast stride out of it. Fast, making a fast march. Instead of the four beats, it was customary, it was playing around New Orleans. We made two beats and a syncopated beat. That's what give it the drive and qualities. Now the musicians that came up from New Orleans, they still would play in ragtime. Many of them followed us up to Chicago. I named them any of the bands. Brown come back the second time, he was still a failure. They had Johnny Fisher's band, he's still a failure. New Orleans band, he was still a failure. Who's that?
